nameStory: The name 'blue-eyed grass' comes from its small, bright blue flowers that look like tiny eyes peering up from grass-like foliage. The word 'strict' refers to its upright, rigid stem that stands straighter than its relatives. It's called 'grass' because of its narrow, blade-like leaves, though it's actually related to irises, not true grasses.
description: Strict blue-eyed grass is a small, grass-like wildflower that forms neat clumps of narrow, upright leaves. Despite its name, it's not a grass at all but a member of the iris family with tiny blue flowers that have yellow centers. The plants typically grow 8-16 inches tall and have flattened, sword-like stems that feel firm and slightly waxy to the touch. Each delicate flower is about half an inch across with six pointed petals.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small blue flowers with six pointed petals and bright yellow centers, about half an inch wide. The petals feel papery and have a subtle sweet fragrance on warm days.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves that are actually flattened and feel stiff and waxy, unlike soft true grass blades. They grow in fan-shaped clumps from the base.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small, neat tufts or clumps that stay low to the ground, with flower stalks rising straight up. The whole plant has a tidy, upright appearance.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Distinctively flattened and winged stems that feel rigid and have sharp edges when you run your finger along them - not round like grass stems.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round seed capsules that split open to reveal tiny dark seeds. The capsules make a subtle rattling sound when shaken when mature.

habitat: Look for strict blue-eyed grass in open, sunny areas with moist to moderately dry soils throughout New England. It thrives in meadows, prairies, open woodlands, and along roadsides where it won't be shaded out by taller plants. You'll often find it growing alongside other wildflowers in areas with good drainage but consistent moisture.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small tufts of narrow leaves. Flower buds begin forming in late spring as distinctive flattened stems shoot up from the leaf clusters.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from late spring through mid-summer, with bright blue flowers opening in the morning sun. Individual flowers last only a day, but new ones keep opening over several weeks.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules ripen and split open, releasing small dark seeds. The leaves begin to yellow and die back, though some may persist into early winter.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back to the ground, leaving only small remnants of the previous year's growth. Look for old seed capsules on dried stems as evidence of their presence.

funFact: Each tiny flower opens only in the morning and closes by afternoon, living for just one day - but the plant is such a prolific bloomer that it can produce flowers continuously for weeks, creating the illusion that the same flowers are blooming day after day.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with actual grasses, but the flattened, sharp-edged stems and six-petaled blue flowers quickly reveal its true identity. Remember: if it has blue flowers and feels like a knife edge, it's blue-eyed grass, not grass!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'grass,' this plant is actually in the iris family, making it a close relative of garden irises and crocuses rather than lawn grass. This common naming confusion happens with many plants that have grass-like leaves but aren't true grasses.
compareHints: Strict blue-eyed grass is very similar to narrow-leaved blue-eyed grass and is sometimes considered the same species. The key difference is that strict blue-eyed grass has more rigidly upright stems and slightly broader leaves. Eastern blue-eyed grass tends to be found in more coastal areas, while strict blue-eyed grass is more common inland and at higher elevations.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Narrow-leaved blue-eyed grass has the thinnest leaves among New England's blue-eyed grasses, typically less than 1/8 inch wide.
Eastern blue-eyed grass can be tricky to distinguish from its close relatives without careful observation.
Coastal Plain Blue-eyed Grass is distinguished from other New England blue-eyed grasses by its preference for sandy coastal soils and its slightly more robust growth habit.

Among New England's blue-eyed grasses, needle-tipped blue-eyed-grass stands out for its truly sharp leaf tips that can pierce skin, while strict blue-eyed grass and narrow-leaved blue-eyed grass have pointed but not needle-sharp leaves.
